question: Why Did My Staging Site Charge Real Customers for Subscription Renewals?
metaDescription: A staging copy of a WooCommerce site can trigger real subscription charges if it isn't properly isolated — here's why, and how to prevent it.
shortAnswer: A staging copy made from a live database keeps every subscription's real payment gateway credentials and scheduled renewal actions intact. If that staging site's cron or Action Scheduler is left running, it will process due renewals exactly like the live site would — charging real customers' real cards from a copy nobody intended to go live. This is a genuine, well-documented risk, not a rare edge case, and it's entirely preventable.

bodyHtml:
Why This Happens

Cloning a WordPress site for staging typically copies the entire database, including live payment gateway API keys, stored customer payment tokens, and every pending Action Scheduler entry for subscription renewals. Nothing about a database clone inherently marks it as "not the real site" — if WP-Cron or a server cron job is active on that staging copy and a renewal happens to be due, it fires exactly as it would in production, using the real gateway credentials it inherited.

This has caught out experienced WooCommerce developers, not just beginners — it's a structural risk in how staging environments are typically created, not a sign of doing something obviously wrong.

Common Causes

  • A full database clone without disabling cron on the staging copy before or immediately after the clone completes.
  • Staging hosting plans that enable WP-Cron by default with no obvious warning that live payment credentials came along with the database.
  • Payment gateway plugins storing live API keys in the database rather than in an environment-specific config file that wouldn't transfer with a simple clone.
  • A staging site left running long-term rather than torn down promptly, increasing the window in which a scheduled renewal could fall due.

How to Prevent It

  1. Disable WP-Cron immediately after cloning to staging, before doing anything else — add define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true); to the staging site's wp-config.php as the very first step.
  2. Switch payment gateways to test/sandbox mode on the staging copy, using sandbox API keys rather than the live account's credentials, so even an accidental charge attempt can't touch real money.
  3. Use a staging tool that automatically handles this — many managed WordPress hosts' staging features switch gateways to test mode or disable cron by default specifically because of this risk; confirm your host's actually does before relying on it.
  4. If a staging site already ran with cron active, check WooCommerce → Status → Scheduled Actions on it immediately and check the live site's actual order/subscription records for any charges that shouldn't exist.
  5. If a real customer was charged from a staging environment, that needs an immediate refund and, if there's a pattern of the same failure recurring, a proper audit of how staging environments get created going forward.

If this has already happened and needs auditing or a hardened staging workflow going forward, see WooCommerce fixes.
